opus-5.5.text:
I think the transition is quite natural, and in some ways almost inevitable. When you work on pretraining for a long time, you're essentially learning how to compress the world's knowledge into a model: data quality, data mixture, scaling laws, architecture, efficiency. But at some point you start to feel that the marginal gains from pretraining alone get harder to see directly. The base model has a lot of latent capability, but it doesn't always express it in the way you want.

Post-training, especially reinforcement learning, is where you actually unlock that capability. It's like the base model has already read a huge library, and post-training teaches it how to think, how to reason step by step, how to use what it knows to solve real problems. When reasoning models came out, many people realized that the ceiling of what a model could do was much higher than we thought, and that a big part of the gain was coming from the post-training stage.

So for a pretraining researcher, moving into post-training is not really switching fields. It's following the bottleneck. A good researcher naturally goes where the biggest open problems are and where their effort has the most leverage. And people with a pretraining background actually bring something valuable. They understand what the base model has and hasn't learned, how data shapes behavior, and how to think about scaling. That intuition helps a lot when designing RL environments, reward signals, or deciding what kind of data to use in post-training.

I also think the boundary between the two is becoming blurrier. Things like mid-training, synthetic reasoning data, and RL at large scale are all connecting the stages. In the end it's one continuous pipeline for building intelligence. The question is less "pretraining or post-training" and more "where is the capability coming from right now, and how do we push it further."

r003.rationale: It describes the move as following the bottleneck and the stages as a continuous pipeline, but does not attribute that movement to flexibility in how researcher roles are defined.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the transition feels natural because the two stages were never really separate problems in researchers' minds. When you do pretraining, you spend years thinking about data: what signal is in the corpus, how the model absorbs it, where its knowledge comes from and where it falls short. Post-training is just a continuation of that same question, except now the data is much smaller, much more deliberate, and you're deciding exactly which capabilities to pull out of the base model and which behaviors to shape.

In the early days, pretraining was where the frontier was. Scaling laws, architecture, data mixtures, training stability at large scale—these were open questions and whoever solved them got the biggest gains. But as the base models matured, a lot of researchers noticed that the ceiling of a model was set in pretraining, while the actual value users experienced was determined in post-training. A base model that knows a lot but can't follow instructions, can't reason step by step, can't refuse gracefully, is not a useful product. So the leverage moved.

There's also a more personal reason. People who did pretraining understand the base model deeply. They know what it has seen, what it is likely to be good at, where it is brittle. That intuition is extremely valuable in post-training, because the hardest part of SFT and RL is diagnosing why a model behaves a certain way and whether the fix belongs in the data, the reward, or back in pretraining. Someone who has only ever done post-training tends to treat the base model as a black box. Someone who came from pretraining treats it as something they built, and they debug it accordingly.

And then reinforcement learning changed the picture again. Once RL with verifiable rewards started producing real reasoning gains, post-training stopped being "alignment polish" and became a genuine scaling axis in its own right—compute, data, and environments all scale, and many of the engineering skills from pretraining transfer directly. So for many researchers it didn't feel like leaving one field for another. It felt like following the compute to where the next unit of improvement actually lives.

r002.rationale: It discusses diagnosing model behavior and choosing a fix, but does not identify inferring algorithm design from model performance as reasoning that data work also involves.

r003.rationale: It explains the transition through continuity between stages and post-training’s growing impact, not flexibility in how researchers’ roles are defined.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a fairly natural transition, because pretraining and post-training are two closely connected parts of building a model. Pretraining gives the model a broad foundation of knowledge and capabilities. Post-training shapes how it uses those capabilities—how it follows instructions, reasons through a problem, and responds to feedback.

If you’ve worked on pretraining, you’re already used to thinking about data quality, optimization, and how to tell whether a change actually improves the model. Those questions remain central in post-training. What changes is the feedback signal. Instead of focusing primarily on predicting the next token, you have to ask: What behavior do we want, and can our training signal reliably encourage it?

I wouldn’t say the transition is effortless, though. A model can learn to score well on a reward without becoming more useful, so evaluation becomes especially important. But the underlying motivation is continuous: you’re still trying to understand how learning produces capability. You’re approaching that question from a different stage of the process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a fairly natural transition, because the underlying goal hasn’t changed: we want to understand how to make models more capable. Pretraining gives a model a broad foundation, while post-training asks how to turn that foundation into behavior that is useful in practice.

Working on pretraining also gives you an intuition for the model’s strengths and limitations. When you move into post-training, you bring that intuition with you: is a problem something the model hasn’t learned, or is it something it knows but doesn’t reliably express? Those lead to different approaches.

But I wouldn’t say post-training is simply an extension of pretraining. The feedback signals and the way you evaluate progress are different. So the transition is natural, but you still have to revisit your assumptions and learn a different set of methods.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes problems the model has not learned from those it does not reliably express, but does not connect inferring algorithm design from performance to reasoning in data work.
